    <div class="guide-header">
        <h1>DORA Compliance Guide 2025 <span class="new-badge"><i class="fas fa-fire"></i> NEW</span></h1>
        <p style="color: var(--text-muted); font-size: 1.1rem;">Complete guide to the Digital Operational Resilience

        <div class="guide-meta" style="margin-top: 1rem;">

    </div>

    <div class="content">
        <h2 id="overview"><i class="fas fa-gavel"></i> 1. What is DORA?</h2>

        <h3>Understanding the Basics</h3>
        <p>Imagine a major bank's computer systems go down for several hours. Customers can't access their money,
            businesses can't process payments, and panic spreads. Now imagine this happening across multiple banks
            simultaneously due to a cyberattack or a failed software update from a shared technology provider.</p>

        <p>This is exactly what <strong>DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act)</strong> is designed to prevent.
            It's like a comprehensive "digital safety rulebook" for the EU financial sector that says: <em>"Your
                technology systems MUST be able to survive problems and keep working."</em></p>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> Think of it like this:</strong> If your car's seatbelt law says
            you must wear a seatbelt, DORA says your financial institution must have a "digital seatbelt" -
            protective measures that keep your technology running safely even when things go wrong.
        </div>

        <h3>The Technical Definition</h3>
        <p>The <strong>Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA)</strong> is a comprehensive EU regulation
            (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554) that establishes a uniform framework for managing ICT (Information and
            Communication Technology) risks across the entire European financial sector.</p>

        <p>DORA aims to ensure that financial entities can:</p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Withstand</strong> - Continue operating during ICT disruptions</li>
            <li><strong>Respond</strong> - Quickly react to cyber incidents and technology failures</li>
            <li><strong>Recover</strong> - Restore normal operations after disruptions</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Why Was DORA Created?</h3>
        <p>Before DORA, EU financial institutions faced a patchwork of inconsistent ICT security requirements spread
            across dozens of different directives. A bank operating in Germany, France, and Spain might face three
            slightly different sets of rules. This created confusion, gaps in protection, and made it harder to
            respond to cross-border incidents.</p>

        <p>Several high-profile incidents highlighted the need for DORA:</p>

        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Year</th>
                    <th>Incident</th>
                    <th>Impact</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td>2018</td>
                    <td>TSB Bank Migration Failure (UK)</td>
                    <td>1.9 million customers locked out for weeks, £330M cost</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>2020</td>
                    <td>SolarWinds Supply Chain Attack</td>
                    <td>Multiple financial institutions affected via third-party software</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>2021</td>
                    <td>AWS Outage</td>
                    <td>Multiple banks and payment processors went offline globally</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>2023</td>
                    <td>ION Trading Ransomware</td>
                    <td>Derivatives trading disrupted across multiple EU financial firms</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> The Wake-Up Call:</strong> The SolarWinds attack in
            particular showed that even if your organization has perfect security, a vulnerability in one of your
            software vendors can compromise your entire operation. DORA specifically addresses this "third-party
            risk" problem.
        </div>

        <h3>What Makes DORA Different?</h3>
        <p>Unlike previous regulations that were <strong>directives</strong> (guidelines that each EU country could
            interpret differently), DORA is a <strong>regulation</strong>. This means:</p>

        <ul>
            <li><strong>Direct applicability:</strong> DORA applies identically in all 27 EU member states - no
                national variations</li>
            <li><strong>No transposition needed:</strong> Member states don't need to pass local laws to implement
                it</li>
            <li><strong>Single rulebook:</strong> Same requirements whether you're in Ireland, Italy, or Estonia
            </li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Core Objectives</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Objective</th>
                    <th>What It Means in Practice</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Harmonization</strong></td>
                    <td>Create one set of ICT risk management rules across all EU financial services - no more
                        confusion about which rules apply where</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Resilience</strong></td>
                    <td>Ensure financial entities can keep operating even when their technology is under attack or
                        experiencing problems</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Oversight</strong></td>
                    <td>Give EU regulators the power to directly supervise critical technology providers (like major
                        cloud services) that support multiple financial institutions</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Transparency</strong></td>
                    <td>Require financial entities to report major ICT incidents so regulators can identify systemic
                        risks and coordinate responses</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Key Takeaway:</strong> DORA represents the EU's most
            comprehensive attempt to protect the financial system from technology-related risks. It recognizes that
            in today's digital world, a cyberattack or IT failure can be just as damaging as a traditional financial
            crisis.
        </div>

        <h2 id="scope"><i class="fas fa-building"></i> 2. Who Must Comply?</h2>
        <p>DORA casts a wide net, covering virtually every type of financial entity in the EU, plus the technology
            companies that serve them.</p>

        <h3>Understanding the Scope (Simple Overview)</h3>
        <p>If you work in finance in the EU and your job involves computers (which is almost everyone today), DORA
            probably applies to your organization. Here's an easy way to think about it:</p>

        <ul>
            <li><strong>Banks and lenders?</strong> <i class="fas fa-check-circle"
                    style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Covered by DORA</li>
            <li><strong>Investment firms?</strong> <i class="fas fa-check-circle"
                    style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Covered by DORA</li>
            <li><strong>Insurance companies?</strong> <i class="fas fa-check-circle"
                    style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Covered by DORA</li>
            <li><strong>Payment processors?</strong> <i class="fas fa-check-circle"
                    style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Covered by DORA</li>
            <li><strong>Crypto exchanges?</strong> <i class="fas fa-check-circle"
                    style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Covered by DORA</li>
            <li><strong>The cloud provider hosting the bank's systems?</strong> <i class="fas fa-check-circle"
                    style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> Also affected by DORA</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Full List of Covered Entities</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Entity Type</th>
                    <th>Examples</th>
                    <th>Compliance Level</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td>Credit Institutions</td>
                    <td>Banks, building societies, credit unions</td>
                    <td>Full</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Investment Firms</td>
                    <td>Broker-dealers, asset managers, hedge funds</td>
                    <td>Full</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Insurance Companies</td>
                    <td>Life insurers, property insurers, reinsurers</td>
                    <td>Full</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Payment Institutions</td>
                    <td>Payment processors, e-money issuers (like Wise, Revolut)</td>
                    <td>Full</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Crypto-Asset Service Providers</td>
                    <td>Crypto exchanges, wallet providers, custodians</td>
                    <td>Full</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Trading Venues</td>
                    <td>Stock exchanges, MTFs, OTFs</td>
                    <td>Full</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Central Counterparties</td>
                    <td>Clearing houses (LCH, Eurex)</td>
                    <td>Full</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Credit Rating Agencies</td>
                    <td>Moody's (EU operations), Fitch, S&P</td>
                    <td>Full</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>ICT Third-Party Providers</td>
                    <td>Cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP), SaaS vendors, IT outsourcers</td>
                    <td>Oversight Framework*</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Small/Micro Entities</td>
                    <td>Fewer than 10 employees, &lt;€2M revenue</td>
                    <td>Simplified**</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-asterisk"></i> Special Notes:</strong>
            <ul style="margin-top: 0.5rem; margin-bottom: 0;">
                <li><strong>*Oversight Framework:</strong> Critical ICT providers designated by EU regulators will
                    be subject to direct EU supervision, not just contractual obligations from their financial
                    clients</li>
                <li><strong>**Simplified:</strong> Small entities get proportionate, less burdensome requirements,
                    but are not exempt</li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <h3>What About Non-EU Companies?</h3>
        <p>DORA primarily applies to entities established in the EU. However, if you're outside the EU but:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>You provide ICT services to EU financial entities → You'll need to comply contractually</li>
            <li>You're designated as a "Critical ICT third-party provider" → You may face direct EU oversight</li>
            <li>You have EU-based subsidiaries → Those subsidiaries must comply</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Pro Tip:</strong> Even if your organization is not directly
            subject to DORA, if you provide ICT services to EU financial entities, you will be indirectly affected.
            Your financial clients will require you to meet DORA standards in your contracts. Start reviewing your
            security practices and contract templates now.
        </div>

        <h2 id="pillars"><i class="fas fa-columns"></i> 3. The 5 Pillars of DORA</h2>
        <p>DORA is structured around five interconnected pillars that together form a comprehensive operational
            resilience framework:</p>

        <div class="pillar-box">
            <h4><span class="pillar-number">1</span> ICT Risk Management</h4>
            <p>Establish and maintain a robust ICT risk management framework with governance, identification,
                protection, detection, response, and recovery capabilities.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="pillar-box">
            <h4><span class="pillar-number">2</span> ICT-Related Incident Reporting</h4>
            <p>Classify, report, and manage ICT-related incidents according to harmonized criteria. Major incidents
                must be reported to competent authorities within strict timelines.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="pillar-box">
            <h4><span class="pillar-number">3</span> Digital Operational Resilience Testing</h4>
            <p>Conduct regular testing of ICT systems including vulnerability assessments, penetration testing, and
                threat-led penetration testing (TLPT) for significant entities.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="pillar-box">
            <h4><span class="pillar-number">4</span> ICT Third-Party Risk Management</h4>
            <p>Manage risks from ICT third-party providers including contractual requirements, ongoing monitoring,
                and exit strategies. Critical providers subject to direct EU oversight.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="pillar-box">
            <h4><span class="pillar-number">5</span> Information Sharing Arrangements</h4>
            <p>Participate in voluntary threat intelligence and information sharing arrangements with other
                financial entities and authorities.</p>
        </div>

        <h2 id="ict-risk"><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i> 4. ICT Risk Management Framework</h2>
        <p>Article 5-16 of DORA establishes comprehensive requirements for ICT risk management. The management body
            (Board/C-suite) bears ultimate responsibility.</p>

        <h3>Governance Requirements</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Management body must approve and oversee the ICT risk management framework</li>
            <li>Allocate sufficient budget for ICT security and resilience</li>
            <li>Appoint an ICT risk management function (separate from internal audit)</li>
            <li>Define, approve, and review ICT security policies at least annually</li>
            <li>Management body members must undergo ICT risk training</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Framework Components</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Component</th>
                    <th>Requirements</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Identification</strong></td>
                    <td>Identify all ICT assets, systems, and their criticality. Document business functions and
                        their ICT dependencies.</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Protection</strong></td>
                    <td>Implement security policies, access controls, encryption, network security, and physical
                        security measures.</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Detection</strong></td>
                    <td>Deploy monitoring capabilities to detect anomalies, intrusions, and ICT-related incidents.
                    </td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Response & Recovery</strong></td>
                    <td>Establish incident response procedures, business continuity plans, and disaster recovery
                        capabilities.</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Learning & Evolution</strong></td>
                    <td>Conduct post-incident reviews, incorporate lessons learned, and continuously improve.</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h2 id="incident-reporting"><i class="fas fa-bell"></i> 5. Incident Reporting Requirements</h2>
        <p>DORA establishes strict incident classification and reporting obligations (Articles 17-23).</p>

        <h3>Incident Classification Criteria</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Number of clients/counterparties affected</li>
            <li>Duration of the incident</li>
            <li>Geographical spread</li>
            <li>Data losses (availability, authenticity, integrity, confidentiality)</li>
            <li>Economic impact</li>
            <li>Criticality of services affected</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-clock"></i> Reporting Timelines:</strong>
            <ul style="margin-top: 0.5rem; margin-bottom: 0;">
                <li><strong>Initial notification:</strong> Within 4 hours of classification (24 hours for
                    non-banking)</li>
                <li><strong>Intermediate report:</strong> Within 72 hours</li>
                <li><strong>Final report:</strong> Within 1 month of incident resolution</li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <h3>What Must Be Reported</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Major ICT-related incidents as classified by DORA criteria</li>
            <li>Significant cyber threats (voluntary but encouraged)</li>
            <li>Incidents at critical ICT third-party providers affecting your operations</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="resilience-testing"><i class="fas fa-vial"></i> 6. Digital Operational Resilience Testing</h2>
        <p>DORA mandates regular testing of ICT systems to validate resilience capabilities (Articles 24-27).</p>

        <h3>Testing Requirements by Entity Type</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Test Type</th>
                    <th>Frequency</th>
                    <th>Applicable To</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td>Vulnerability Assessments</td>
                    <td>Continuous / Regular</td>
                    <td>All entities</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Network Security Testing</td>
                    <td>At least annually</td>
                    <td>All entities</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Penetration Testing</td>
                    <td>At least annually</td>
                    <td>All entities</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Source Code Review</td>
                    <td>For critical systems</td>
                    <td>All entities</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Scenario-Based Testing</td>
                    <td>At least annually</td>
                    <td>All entities</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Threat-Led Penetration Testing (TLPT)</td>
                    <td>Every 3 years minimum</td>
                    <td>Significant entities only</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h3>TLPT Requirements</h3>
        <p>Threat-Led Penetration Testing based on the TIBER-EU framework is required for systemically important
            financial entities:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>Must use external (independent) testers</li>
            <li>Based on real threat intelligence</li>
            <li>Cover critical or important functions</li>
            <li>Include ICT third-party providers (with their agreement)</li>
            <li>Competent authorities must be notified and may participate</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="third-party"><i class="fas fa-handshake"></i> 7. Third-Party ICT Risk Management</h2>
        <p>DORA places significant emphasis on managing risks from ICT service providers (Articles 28-44).</p>

        <h3>Pre-Contractual Due Diligence</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Assess provider's ability to meet DORA requirements</li>
            <li>Evaluate concentration risk (over-reliance on single providers)</li>
            <li>Consider substitutability and exit strategies</li>
            <li>Review provider's security certifications and audit reports</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Mandatory Contractual Provisions</h3>
        <p>All ICT service contracts must include:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>Clear description of services and performance levels (SLAs)</li>
            <li>Location of data processing and storage</li>
            <li>Provisions on data protection and access</li>
            <li>Right to audit and access</li>
            <li>Incident notification obligations</li>
            <li>Exit strategies and transition assistance</li>
            <li>Subcontracting conditions and limits</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-eye"></i> Oversight Framework:</strong> Critical ICT third-party providers
            (designated by ESAs) are subject to direct EU oversight including on-site inspections, recommendations,
            and ultimately the power to impose penalties.
        </div>

        <h3>Register of ICT Third-Party Providers</h3>
        <p>Financial entities must maintain a register of all ICT third-party arrangements containing:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>Provider identification details</li>
            <li>Services provided and criticality assessment</li>
            <li>Contract details and duration</li>
            <li>Subcontractors and fourth-party dependencies</li>
            <li>Data locations</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="information-sharing"><i class="fas fa-share-alt"></i> 8. Information Sharing Arrangements</h2>
        <p>DORA encourages participation in cyber threat intelligence sharing (Article 45).</p>

        <h3>Benefits of Participation</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Early warning of emerging threats</li>
            <li>Access to indicators of compromise (IOCs)</li>
            <li>Collaborative defense against common adversaries</li>
            <li>Benchmarking security practices</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Requirements for Sharing Arrangements</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Protect confidentiality of shared information</li>
            <li>Handle personal data in compliance with GDPR</li>
            <li>Notify competent authorities of participation</li>
            <li>Define governance and liability frameworks</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="timeline"><i class="fas fa-calendar-check"></i> 9. Implementation Timeline</h2>

        <div class="timeline">
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">December 2022</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">DORA officially published in the Official Journal of the EU</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">January 2023</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">DORA enters into force (20 days after publication)</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">2023-2024</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">ESAs (EBA, EIOPA, ESMA) develop Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS)
                    and Implementing Technical Standards (ITS)</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">July 2024</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">First batch of RTS adopted by European Commission</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item"
                style="background: rgba(255, 215, 0, 0.1); padding: 1rem; border-radius: 8px; margin-left: -1rem;">
                <span class="timeline-date" style="font-size: 1.1rem;">January 17, 2025</span>
                <span class="timeline-event"><strong>DORA BECOMES FULLY APPLICABLE</strong> - All requirements must
                    be implemented</span>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h2 id="checklist"><i class="fas fa-tasks"></i> 10. Compliance Checklist</h2>

        <h3>ICT Risk Management</h3>
        <ul class="checklist">
            <li>Establish ICT risk management framework approved by management body</li>
            <li>Document all ICT assets, systems, and dependencies</li>
            <li>Implement ICT security policies covering all DORA domains</li>
            <li>Deploy detection and monitoring capabilities</li>
            <li>Develop and test business continuity and disaster recovery plans</li>
            <li>Allocate dedicated budget for ICT security</li>
            <li>Provide ICT risk training to management body</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Incident Management</h3>
        <ul class="checklist">
            <li>Implement incident classification process per DORA criteria</li>
            <li>Establish incident response procedures</li>
            <li>Create reporting templates and escalation paths</li>
            <li>Configure systems for 4-hour reporting capability</li>
            <li>Document post-incident review process</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Resilience Testing</h3>
        <ul class="checklist">
            <li>Schedule annual penetration tests and vulnerability assessments</li>
            <li>Plan TLPT if classified as significant entity</li>
            <li>Document testing scope, results, and remediation</li>
            <li>Include critical ICT providers in testing scope</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Third-Party Risk</h3>
        <ul class="checklist">
            <li>Create register of all ICT third-party agreements</li>
            <li>Review and update contracts with mandatory DORA clauses</li>
            <li>Assess concentration risk across providers</li>
            <li>Develop exit strategies for critical providers</li>
            <li>Establish ongoing monitoring of provider security</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="penalties"><i class="fas fa-gavel"></i> 11. Penalties for Non-Compliance</h2>
        <p>DORA empowers competent authorities to impose significant penalties:</p>

        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Violation Type</th>
                    <th>Potential Penalties</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td>Minor Infringements</td>
                    <td>Public warnings, orders to cease conduct, administrative fines</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Significant Infringements</td>
                    <td>Fines up to €5 million or 10% of annual turnover (for entities)</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Individual Liability</td>
                    <td>Fines up to €500,000 for responsible persons</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Critical ICT Providers</td>
                    <td>Periodic penalty payments up to 1% of daily worldwide turnover</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Next Steps:</strong>
            <ol style="margin-top: 0.5rem; margin-bottom: 0;">
                <li>Conduct a DORA gap assessment against current practices</li>
                <li>Prioritize gaps based on risk and implementation effort</li>
                <li>Update contracts with ICT providers to include DORA clauses</li>
                <li>Implement or enhance incident reporting capabilities</li>
                <li>Schedule required testing activities</li>
            </ol>
        </div>
